title: Universal Monsters & Gothic Fear
thematicFocus: Gothic escapism, romanticized monsters, external threats.
culturalContext: Born during the Great Depression and World War II, horror allowed audiences to project real-world anxieties onto fantastical, distant creatures. Monsters were symbolic and physically distinct from normal human society.

title: Psychological Shift & Visceral Terror
thematicFocus: Real-world violence, domestic terror, loss of institutional trust.
culturalContext: Civil rights unrest, the Vietnam War, and the decay of the suburban nuclear family brought terror into domestic spaces. The monster became a neighbor or masked killer.

title: Slasher Boom & The Satanic Panic
thematicFocus: Franchise morality plays, practical gore, censorship, and moral panic.
culturalContext: The rise of VHS led to mass-market slasher franchises. Concurrently, conservative social movements and the Satanic Panic forced heavy censorship, leading to formulaic sequels.

title: Postmodern Revival
culturalContext: Following 1980s oversaturation, horror became self-conscious. Films like Scream began deconstructing genre tropes for a media-literate generation raised on slashers.

title: Extreme Realism & Torture Cinema
thematicFocus: Visceral vulnerability, post-9/11 anxiety, surveillance, and body horror.
culturalContext: Post-9/11 anxiety and 24-hour news coverage fueled claustrophobic violence (Saw, Hostel) alongside techno-dread Asian horror remakes (The Ring). Fear shifted toward systemic entrapment and helpless suffering.

title: Blockbuster Haunted Houses & Elevated Horror
thematicFocus: Mainstream cinematic universes vs. grief, trauma, and auteur dread.
culturalContext: The genre split into studio haunted house franchises for mass audiences (The Conjuring) and indie elevated horror exploring grief, generational trauma, and psychological decay (Hereditary, Midsommar, Get Out).
